note: Original self-check quizzes written for MGA. A quiz is a self-check, not proof of skill. No links; resources come only from resources.json.

questions.question: After building a prefix-sum array once in O(n), how long does each later 'sum of elements from index i to j' query take?
options: O(j - i) in the worst case
questions.explain: Each range sum is prefix[j+1] - prefix[i], two lookups and one subtraction.

questions.question: What is the minimum time needed to find the largest value in an unsorted array of n numbers?
options: O(n), because every element must be looked at
O(1), if you keep a pointer to the end
O(log n), by halving the array
O(n log n), because sorting is required
questions.explain: Without order, any unchecked element could be the maximum, so all n must be inspected.

questions.question: You reverse an array in place by swapping the first and last elements, then moving both indices inward. How much extra memory does this use besides the array?
options: O(n / 2) for a temporary copy of half the array
questions.explain: Only the two indices and one temporary value are needed, regardless of n.

questions.question: Pseudocode: counts = array of 26 zeros; for each letter c in "abca": counts[c] = counts[c] + 1. How many entries of counts are non-zero afterwards?
questions.explain: The letters present are a (twice), b and c, so three distinct entries are non-zero.

questions.question: Inserting a new element at the very front of a dynamic array holding n elements costs, in the worst case:
options: O(n), because every existing element shifts one place
O(1), because arrays have direct access
O(1) amortised, same as appending at the end
questions.explain: Each element must move to make room at index 0; only appending at the end is amortised O(1).

questions.question: In a language where strings are immutable, you build a string of length n by appending one character at a time in a loop. What is the total time, assuming each append copies the whole string?
questions.explain: The copies cost 1 + 2 + ... + n characters, which is about n^2 / 2.

questions.question: What is the average-case time of looking up a key in a well-designed hash map?
questions.explain: A good hash function spreads keys so each lookup touches a constant number of entries on average.

questions.question: A hash map uses separate chaining with plain linked lists in each bucket. If every key lands in the same bucket, one lookup takes:
questions.explain: All n entries sit in a single list that must be scanned.

questions.question: Which rule must a hash function used for map keys always follow?
options: The original key must be recoverable from its hash
Hash values must come out in sorted order
Two equal keys must produce the same hash value
Two different keys must always produce different hash values
questions.explain: Equal keys going to different buckets would make lookups fail. Collisions between different keys are allowed.

questions.question: Pseudocode: seen = empty set; dupes = 0; for x in [3, 5, 3, 7, 5]: if x in seen then dupes = dupes + 1 else add x to seen. What is dupes at the end?
questions.explain: The second 3 and the second 5 are repeats; 7 appears once.

questions.question: Using a hash map in one left-to-right pass, you look for two numbers in an unsorted array that add up to a target. What are the time and extra space?
options: O(n log n) time and O(n) space
questions.explain: Each element needs one map lookup for its complement and one insert, and the map can hold up to n entries.

questions.question: A mutable list is used as a map key and its contents are changed after insertion. What is the likely problem?
options: Its hash changes, so the entry may no longer be found where it was stored
The map automatically moves the entry to the correct bucket
Nothing; keys are copied on insertion
The map becomes sorted by the new contents
questions.explain: The entry stays in the bucket chosen from the old hash, so a lookup with the new hash looks elsewhere.

questions.question: Array sorted ascending. One pointer is at each end and you want a pair summing to a target. The current sum is larger than the target. What do you do?
options: Move the left pointer one step right
Move the right pointer one step left
questions.explain: Moving the right pointer left lowers the sum. Moving the left pointer right would only raise it.

questions.question: What are the time and extra space of the opposite-end two-pointer pair search on a sorted array of n numbers?
options: O(log n) time and O(1) space
questions.explain: Each pointer moves in one direction at most n steps in total, and only two indices are stored.

questions.question: You need the sum of every window of k consecutive elements in an array of n. Keeping a running sum, adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one, makes the whole job:
questions.explain: Each slide costs a constant amount of work instead of re-adding k elements.

questions.question: A linked list has 7 nodes and no cycle. A slow pointer moves 1 step and a fast pointer moves 2 steps per round, both starting at node 1. When the fast pointer reaches the last node (node 7), which node is the slow pointer on?
questions.explain: After t rounds slow is at node 1 + t and fast at 1 + 2t. Fast is at node 7 when t = 3, so slow is at node 4, the middle.

questions.question: Finding the longest substring with no repeated characters using a variable window. A new character is already inside the window. What do you do?
options: Move the left edge forward until the earlier copy is outside the window
Skip the new character and keep the window unchanged
Move the right edge back one step
Clear the whole window and restart at the new character
questions.explain: Shrinking from the left removes the old copy and keeps the window valid while preserving earlier progress.

questions.question: Pseudocode: arr = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]; write = 1; for read from 1 to 4: if arr[read] != arr[read - 1] then arr[write] = arr[read]; write = write + 1. What is write at the end?
questions.explain: The value changes at index 2 (1 to 2) and at index 4 (2 to 3), so write goes from 1 to 3. The first 3 entries are 1, 2, 3.

questions.question: What is the worst-case number of comparisons binary search needs on a sorted array of n elements?
questions.explain: Each comparison halves the remaining range.

questions.question: Binary search on a sorted array with indices 0 to 9 (10 elements) computes mid = (lo + hi) / 2 using integer division. Which index is checked first?
questions.explain: (0 + 9) / 2 = 4 with integer division.

questions.question: You want to use 'binary search on the answer' to find the smallest X that makes a check pass. What must be true of the check?
options: If it passes for some X, it also passes for every larger X
It must pass for exactly one value of X
It must pass for every even X
The values must be stored in an array first
questions.explain: Binary search needs a monotonic condition so that one test tells you which half to discard.

questions.question: What are the worst-case time and extra space of merge sort on n elements (standard array version)?
options: O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space
O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space
O(n) time and O(n) extra space
O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space
questions.explain: It splits log n times, merges n elements per level, and needs a temporary array to merge.

questions.question: A sort is called stable. What does that guarantee?
options: Its running time is always the same
Items with equal keys keep their original relative order
It works on already sorted data only
questions.explain: Stability matters, for example, when you sort by one field after sorting by another.

questions.question: Quicksort always uses the first element as the pivot. On an array that is already sorted, the running time is:
questions.explain: The pivot is always the smallest, so each partition removes just one element, giving n + (n-1) + ... + 1 steps.

questions.question: How long does it take to read the element at position k of a singly linked list, given only the head pointer?
questions.explain: There is no index arithmetic; you follow next pointers one at a time.

questions.question: You already hold a pointer to a node in a singly linked list. Inserting a new node right after it takes:
questions.explain: Only two pointer updates are needed: the new node's next and the existing node's next.

questions.question: Pseudocode: prev = null; cur = head; while cur != null: nxt = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt; return prev. The list is 1 -> 2 -> 3. What is the value of the node returned?
questions.explain: This reverses the list, so the old tail (3) becomes the new head.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a dummy head node in list problems such as deleting a value?
options: It allows random access by index
It removes the need to follow next pointers
The head no longer needs special-case code
questions.explain: With a dummy in front, deleting the first real node is handled the same as deleting any other.

questions.question: Floyd's fast and slow pointer method detects a cycle in a linked list using how much extra memory?
questions.explain: It stores two pointers only, unlike a visited-set approach that can hold all n nodes.

questions.question: Why is binary search a poor fit for a sorted linked list?
options: Reaching the middle node takes O(n), so there is no speedup from halving
Binary search needs the list to be doubly linked
Linked lists cannot store sorted data
Comparisons are more expensive on linked lists
questions.explain: Each halving step still requires walking along the links, so the total work stays linear.

questions.question: Operations on an empty stack: push 1, push 2, push 3, pop, pop, push 4, pop. What does the last pop return?
questions.explain: After the two pops the stack is [1]; push 4 gives [1, 4], and pop returns the top, 4.

questions.question: Operations on an empty queue: enqueue A, enqueue B, enqueue C, dequeue, enqueue D, dequeue. What does the last dequeue return?
questions.explain: A queue is first-in first-out: A leaves first, then B.

questions.question: Which of these bracket strings is balanced?
questions.explain: Every bracket is closed by the matching type in the correct nesting order only in {[()]}.

questions.question: Finding the next greater element for every item in an array with a monotonic stack takes what total time?
options: O(n), because each element is pushed and popped at most once
questions.explain: Although there is a loop inside a loop, the total number of pops cannot exceed the number of pushes.

questions.question: You implement a queue using two stacks (one for input, one for output, moving items over only when the output stack is empty). The amortised cost per operation is:
questions.explain: Each element is moved at most once between stacks, so the occasional O(n) transfer is spread across many operations.

questions.question: Which pairing of traversal and structure is correct for an iterative graph search?
options: Depth-first with a queue, breadth-first with a stack
Depth-first with a stack, breadth-first with a queue
questions.explain: A stack explores the most recent neighbour first (deep), a queue explores level by level.

questions.question: Pseudocode: f(n): if n == 0 return 0; return n + f(n - 1). What does f(4) return?
What happens if a recursive function has no reachable base case?
options: It keeps calling itself until the call stack overflows
The compiler rewrites it as a loop
questions.explain: Each call adds a stack frame, and the stack is finite.

questions.question: A naive recursive fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) with base cases fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1 runs in about:
questions.explain: The same subproblems are recomputed many times, so the number of calls roughly doubles with each extra level.

questions.question: How many subsets (including the empty set and the full set) does a set of 5 distinct elements have?
questions.explain: Each element is either in or out: 2^5 = 32.

questions.question: How many different orderings (permutations) exist for 4 distinct items?
In backtracking, what is the purpose of the 'un-choose' step after exploring one choice?
options: To store the answer found so far
To make the search faster by skipping branches
To restore the state so the next choice starts from a clean position
questions.explain: Without undoing the change, later branches would see leftovers from earlier ones and produce wrong results.

questions.question: What is the extra memory used by a recursive depth-first traversal of a binary tree of height h (not counting the tree itself)?
questions.explain: The recursion goes at most h levels deep. For a skewed tree h can be n.

questions.question: An in-order traversal of a valid binary search tree visits the keys in what order?
questions.explain: Left subtree, then node, then right subtree matches the BST ordering rule.

questions.question: A binary tree is completely full and has 3 levels (the root is level 1). How many nodes does it have?
A tree has root 1 with children 2 (left) and 3 (right). Node 2 has a left child 4 and no right child. What does a post-order traversal (left, right, node) print?
questions.explain: Under 2: print 4 then 2. Then the right subtree 3. The root 1 comes last.

questions.question: Which data structure does a level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a tree use?
questions.explain: A queue processes nodes in the order they were discovered, which gives level by level.

questions.question: You insert the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order into a plain (non-balancing) binary search tree. What is the cost of searching for 5 afterwards?
options: O(n), because the tree is a chain
questions.explain: Each key becomes the right child of the previous one, so the tree degenerates into a linked list.

questions.question: In a binary min-heap, where is the smallest element and how long does it take to read it?
options: At a leaf, in O(log n)
At the root, in O(log n)
questions.explain: The heap property puts the minimum at the root; peeking does not change the heap.

questions.question: How long do push and pop (remove the minimum) take in a binary heap of n elements?
questions.explain: The new or moved element sifts through at most the height of the tree, about log2(n) levels.

questions.question: To get the K largest of n numbers you keep a min-heap of at most K items, pushing each number and popping when the size exceeds K. The time is:
questions.explain: Each of n numbers causes at most one push and one pop on a heap of size K.

questions.question: Building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements with the bottom-up method takes:
questions.explain: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift only a short distance, which sums to a linear total.

questions.question: A binary heap is stored in an array with 0-based indices, and the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. What is the parent of index 5?
questions.explain: Index 2 has children 2*2 + 1 = 5 and 2*2 + 2 = 6, so the parent of 5 is 2, which is (5 - 1) / 2 with integer division.

questions.question: To maintain a running median with two heaps, what does the max-heap hold?
options: The smaller half of the numbers
The larger half of the numbers
questions.explain: The max-heap root is the largest of the lower half, and the min-heap root is the smallest of the upper half; the median comes from these roots.

questions.question: How much memory does an adjacency list for a graph with V vertices and E edges use?
questions.explain: One list header per vertex plus one entry per edge (two per edge if undirected).

questions.question: In an unweighted graph, which algorithm finds the path with the fewest edges from a source to every other vertex?
questions.explain: BFS visits vertices in order of increasing distance from the source.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS on a graph stored as an adjacency list?
questions.explain: Each vertex is dequeued once and each edge is examined a constant number of times.

questions.question: A topological ordering of a directed graph exists only if the graph:
options: Has the same number of vertices and edges
questions.explain: A cycle means a set of tasks each waiting for another, so no valid order can exist.

questions.question: Directed edges: A->B, A->C, B->D, C->D. Which of these is a valid topological order?
questions.explain: Every edge goes forward in A B C D. The others put a vertex before one that must precede it.

questions.question: Doing DFS on an undirected graph, you reach an already-visited vertex that is not the vertex you just came from. What does this show?
questions.explain: There are now two different paths between the same two vertices, which forms a cycle.

questions.question: To pick the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings, which greedy rule is correct?
options: Choose the meeting that overlaps the most others
Choose the meeting that starts earliest
Repeatedly choose the compatible meeting that finishes earliest
questions.explain: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest. Shortest-first and earliest-start both have counterexamples.

questions.question: When can a greedy algorithm be trusted to give an optimal answer?
options: When a locally best choice can always be extended to a globally optimal solution
Always, if it runs in O(n log n)
Whenever the problem asks for a minimum
questions.explain: That 'greedy choice' property has to be argued for each problem, usually with an exchange argument.

questions.question: Coins are {1, 3, 4} and you always take the largest coin that fits. How many coins does this give for an amount of 6?
questions.explain: Greedy takes 4 first and then needs two 1s. This shows greedy is not optimal for every coin set.

questions.question: Meetings (start, end): (1,3), (2,4), (3,5), (6,7). A meeting that ends at 3 and another that starts at 3 do not conflict. What is the maximum number you can attend?
questions.explain: Take (1,3), then (3,5), then (6,7). (2,4) overlaps with both (1,3) and (3,5).

questions.question: Greedy interval scheduling sorts n meetings by end time and then scans once. The total running time is:
questions.explain: The sort dominates; the scan afterwards is linear.

questions.question: What is an 'exchange argument' used for in greedy proofs?
options: To test the algorithm on random inputs
To show that swapping an optimal solution's choice for the greedy choice does not make it worse
questions.explain: Repeating the swap transforms any optimal solution into the greedy one without losing quality.

questions.question: Which two properties together suggest that dynamic programming will work for a problem?
options: A graph with no cycles and positive weights
A single loop and constant memory
questions.explain: Subproblems repeat (so caching helps) and the best answer is built from best answers to smaller problems.

questions.question: Adding memoisation to naive recursive Fibonacci changes the time from exponential to:
questions.explain: Each of the n distinct values is computed once, then reused.

questions.question: You can climb 1 or 2 stairs at a time, with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2, and ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2). What is ways(5)?
questions.explain: ways(3) = 3, ways(4) = 5, ways(5) = 8.

questions.question: A robot moves from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 3 x 3 grid of cells, moving only right or down. How many different paths are there?
questions.explain: It makes 2 right and 2 down moves in some order: 4 moves choose 2 = 6.

questions.question: For the longest common subsequence of strings of lengths n and m, the standard table approach takes:
questions.explain: There is one table cell per pair of prefixes, each filled in constant time.

questions.question: A 0/1 knapsack has n items and capacity W. The standard dynamic programming solution takes:
questions.explain: The table has n rows and W + 1 columns. This is pseudo-polynomial because W is a number, not an input size.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm gives correct shortest paths only if the edge weights are:
questions.explain: A negative edge can make an already-finalised vertex reachable more cheaply later.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with V vertices and E edges, using a binary heap, runs in about:
questions.explain: Each edge can cause one heap push, and each heap operation costs O(log V).

questions.question: Undirected weighted edges: A-B 4, A-C 1, C-B 2, B-D 1. What is the shortest distance from A to D?
questions.explain: A-C-B-D costs 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. The direct route A-B-D costs 4 + 1 = 5.

questions.question: A union-find (disjoint set) structure uses path compression and union by rank. The amortised cost of each operation is:
questions.explain: The combined optimisations keep trees so flat that the cost is effectively constant for any realistic n.

questions.question: How many edges does a minimum spanning tree of a connected graph with V vertices have?
questions.explain: A spanning tree connects V vertices with no cycle, which takes exactly V - 1 edges.

questions.question: In Kruskal's algorithm, which rule decides whether the next cheapest edge is added?
options: Add it only if its endpoints are in different components
Add it only if it is connected to the last added edge
Add it only if it is shorter than the average edge
questions.explain: Joining two vertices already connected would create a cycle, which a tree cannot have.

questions.question: In a trie, looking up a word of length L takes how long, ignoring the alphabet size?
options: O(log n) where n is the number of words
questions.explain: You follow one edge per character, no matter how many words are stored.

questions.question: Pseudocode: result = 0; for x in [4, 7, 4, 9, 7]: result = result XOR x. What is result?
questions.explain: XOR of equal values cancels (a XOR a = 0), so 4, 4 and 7, 7 cancel and only 9 remains.

questions.question: What is 12 AND 11 (that is, n AND (n - 1) with n = 12)? Binary: 12 = 1100, 11 = 1011.
questions.explain: 1100 AND 1011 = 1000, which is 8. The operation clears the lowest set bit.

questions.question: Why can a trie answer 'does any stored word start with this prefix?' better than a hash set of words?
options: A trie stores words in sorted order only
Following the prefix's characters reaches a node covering all words with that prefix
questions.explain: A hash set only answers exact matches; a trie keeps shared prefixes together in its structure.

questions.question: What is 5 left-shifted by 2 (5 << 2)?
questions.explain: Shifting left by k multiplies by 2^k: 5 x 4 = 20.

questions.question: A trie stores several words with a total of N characters across all of them. At most how many nodes does it have, not counting the root?
questions.explain: Each character adds at most one new node, and shared prefixes only reduce that.

questions.question: What does encapsulation mean?
options: Creating a new class from an existing one
Using one method name for several different tasks
Keeping an object's internal state private and exposing it through methods
Running several objects at the same time
questions.explain: Hiding state lets the class protect its rules, for example never allowing a negative balance.

questions.question: Pseudocode: class Animal has speak() that prints "...". class Dog extends Animal and overrides speak() to print "woof". Then: a = new Dog(); a.speak() where a is declared as type Animal. In a language with dynamic dispatch, what prints?
options: Nothing; it is a compile error
questions.explain: The method that runs is chosen from the real object type (Dog) at run time. This is polymorphism.

questions.question: A Car contains an Engine object it uses to move. Which relationship is this?
questions.explain: A car is not a kind of engine; it has one. Prefer composition when the relationship is not truly is-a.

questions.question: Which statement about method overriding is correct?
options: A subclass supplies its own version of a method defined in its parent with the same signature
Two methods with the same name but different parameters are in the same class
A method that is only available at compile time
A method that cannot be called from outside the class
questions.explain: The second option describes overloading, the third describes a private method.

questions.question: The Single Responsibility Principle says that a class should:
options: Have only one reason to change
Be used by only one other class
questions.explain: Mixing unrelated duties (for example billing and email formatting) makes changes to one risk breaking the other.

questions.question: A class declares an abstract method with no body. What follows from this?
options: Objects of the class can be created but the method returns null
The method is called automatically by subclasses
The class cannot be instantiated directly; a concrete subclass must implement the method
questions.explain: Abstract methods define what subclasses must provide, so the class is incomplete on its own.

questions.question: Threads of the same process share which of these by default?
questions.explain: Each thread has its own stack and registers, but they all see the same process address space.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four conditions needed for a deadlock?
questions.explain: The conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Scheduling policy is not on the list.

questions.question: What happens during a context switch?
options: The CPU state of the running process is saved and the state of another process is loaded
questions.explain: This lets the OS share one CPU among many processes.

questions.question: A page fault occurs when:
options: Two processes use the same file
A process accesses a page that is not currently in physical memory
questions.explain: The OS has to bring the page in (from disk, for example) before the instruction can continue.

questions.question: Round-robin scheduling, time quantum 4 ms. P1, P2, P3 all arrive at time 0 in that order, each needing 8 ms of CPU. At what time does P1 finish?
questions.explain: P1 runs 0-4, P2 4-8, P3 8-12, then P1 runs again 12-16 and completes.

questions.question: Two threads each run counter = counter + 1 a thousand times on a shared variable with no locking. Why might the final value be below 2000?
options: The read-add-write steps of the two threads can interleave, so some updates are lost
Threads can only run one after the other, so the second overwrites the first
The OS skips every other instruction
questions.explain: This is a race condition; a mutex or an atomic increment makes the update safe.

questions.question: What does a primary key guarantee in a table?
options: Each row can be identified uniquely and the key is never NULL
The column can only hold numbers
The table is sorted by that column
questions.explain: Uniqueness and non-null are required; sorting and types are separate concerns.

questions.question: In ACID, what does the letter I stand for and what does it protect against?
options: Isolation, so concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work
Integrity, so numbers are always positive
Inheritance, so tables extend each other
questions.explain: Isolation gives each transaction the effect of running alone, to a degree set by the isolation level.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of normalisation?
options: To reduce duplicated data and the update anomalies it causes
To store data as one large table
To make queries run faster in all cases
questions.explain: Storing each fact once avoids having to update several copies that may become inconsistent.

questions.question: Which describes the usual trade-off of adding an index to a column?
options: Writes get faster and reads get slower
Reads and writes both get faster
Reads on that column get faster, but writes get slower and storage grows
questions.explain: Every insert, update or delete must also maintain the index structure.

questions.question: An orders table has a column customer_id declared as a foreign key to customers(id). What does this enforce?
options: Every customer must have at least one order
Every order must refer to a customer that exists
questions.explain: This is referential integrity; it blocks orders pointing to missing customers.

questions.question: A transfer debits account A by 500 and then the system crashes before crediting account B. Which ACID property ensures the debit is undone?
questions.explain: Atomicity means the transaction happens completely or not at all, so the partial debit is rolled back.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares TCP and UDP?
options: TCP is connection-oriented with ordered, retransmitted delivery; UDP sends datagrams with no such guarantees
UDP guarantees delivery and TCP does not
TCP is used only for email
questions.explain: UDP trades reliability for lower overhead, which suits things like live audio.

questions.question: What is the job of DNS?
options: To translate domain names into IP addresses
To assign a MAC address to each device
questions.explain: Browsers use names; the network needs IP addresses.

questions.question: An HTTP response has status code 503. What class of problem does this indicate?
questions.explain: 5xx codes mean the server failed or is unavailable, even if the request was valid.

questions.question: What is the sequence of the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.explain: The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with ACK.

questions.question: What does HTTPS add on top of plain HTTP?
options: Encryption of the traffic and authentication of the server through TLS and certificates
A guarantee that the website content is true
A faster protocol that skips DNS
questions.explain: TLS protects the connection, but it says nothing about whether the site itself is honest.

questions.question: How many addresses are in the IPv4 block 192.168.1.0/24, counting every address?
questions.explain: A /24 leaves 8 host bits, so 2^8 = 256 addresses. (Usually 254 are usable for hosts.)

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling?
options: Handling more load by adding more machines
Giving one machine more CPU and RAM
questions.explain: Adding more CPU or RAM to one machine is vertical scaling.

questions.question: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?
options: The application reads from the database and then stores the result in the cache
The cache calls the database itself and returns an error
questions.explain: The application is responsible for loading the cache, so later reads for the same key are fast.

questions.question: During a network partition between two replicas of a database, the CAP theorem says a system must choose between:
questions.explain: When replicas cannot talk, answering requests risks stale data, while refusing requests loses availability.

questions.question: What does a load balancer do?
options: Spreads incoming requests across several servers
questions.explain: It also helps hide failed servers by routing around them.

questions.question: A service receives about 1 million requests per day, evenly spread. Roughly how many requests per second is that on average?
questions.explain: There are 86,400 seconds in a day: 1,000,000 / 86,400 is about 11.6. Peak traffic is usually several times higher.

questions.question: A client times out on a payment request and retries it. What property should the server's payment endpoint have so the customer is not charged twice?
options: Idempotency, using a unique request key to recognise repeats
questions.explain: With an idempotency key the server returns the earlier result instead of charging again.

questions.question: Which statement about WHERE and HAVING is correct?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
WHERE can only be used with joins
HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters groups
questions.explain: Aggregate conditions such as SUM(amount) > 100 belong in HAVING.

questions.question: Table students(id) and table marks(student_id, score). A student with no marks should still appear in the result, with NULL for score. Which join does this?
options: Any join; they behave the same
questions.explain: A left join keeps every row from the left table and fills missing matches with NULL.

questions.question: Table t has column x with the values 1, 2, NULL, 4. What does SELECT COUNT(x) FROM t return?
questions.explain: COUNT(column) ignores NULLs. COUNT(*) would return 4.

questions.question: What does SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = NULL return?
questions.explain: A comparison with NULL is never true. Use city IS NULL instead.

questions.question: Table orders(customer, amount) has rows (A, 100), (A, 50), (B, 70). The query is: SELECT customer FROM orders GROUP BY customer HAVING SUM(amount) > 100. What does it return?
questions.explain: A totals 150 (above 100) and B totals 70 (not above 100).

questions.question: A plain B-tree index exists on column email. Which query can use it most effectively for a fast lookup?
questions.explain: An exact match on the indexed value works. Wrapping the column in a function or starting the pattern with a wildcard prevents a plain index from being used.
